title: Nvidia Opens 18.9M Nemotron Parse Training Examples, DFlash2
summary: Nvidia released 18.9M synthetic training examples for Nemotron 3.5 Parse and an 89.3M-parameter DFlash2 speculator, boosting document parsing throughput to
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Nvidia released 18.88M synthetic training examples for Nemotron 3.5 Parse under the commercial-friendly OpenMDW 1.1 license on November 26, 2026.
- The bundle includes a fine-tuning recipe and an 89.3M-parameter DFlash2 drafter that boosts parsing throughput up to 7.62x on a single H200.
- RAG and agent teams can now adapt the open document parser to custom forms and languages using the reproducible training recipe.


Nvidia opened the complete training pipeline behind its Nemotron 3.5 Parse document model on November 26, 2026, releasing 18.88 million synthetic examples, a full fine-tuning recipe, and a new 89.3-million-parameter DFlash2 speculative-decoding drafter under the commercial-friendly OpenMDW 1.1 license. The release, published in a Hugging Face blog by Ryan Chesler, Marek Wawrzos, and Steve Han, gives RAG and agent teams everything they need to adapt a production-grade document parser to their own forms, languages, and layouts.


Officially launched on November 26, 2026, the data package addresses a persistent bottleneck in enterprise AI: extracting structured text, tables, and charts from page images at scale. Nemotron 3.5 Parse, first released in October 2026, is a 0.631-billion-parameter model that converts a page image into reading-order text with content classes (headings, paragraphs, tables, charts) and bounding boxes, optimized for retrieval-augmented generation and agent workflows.


## Three Synthetic Datasets Totaling 18.88M Examples


The training corpus comprises three datasets designed to cover the full spectrum of document understanding. Synthetic Charts V1 provides 9.98 million rendered charts with category, series, and value annotations. Synthetic Tables V1 delivers 1 million HTML tables preserving row, column, header, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 adds 7.9 million synthetic pages with varied fonts and layouts for multilingual OCR training.


All three datasets are available on Hugging Face under OpenMDW 1.1, permitting commercial use without additional licensing friction. The release includes image-label pairs, generation scripts, and a full NeMo Automodel SFT pipeline, so teams can reproduce or extend the training process for domain-specific forms.


## Two-Phase Training: SFT Plus Reinforcement Learning


Nvidia trained Parse in two phases. Supervised fine-tuning covered text extraction, layout analysis, table parsing, chart interpretation, and multilingual OCR. The second phase applied reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) via GRPO, where rewards check extraction quality by verifying correct series and values, usable structure, and completion without looping.


On development checkpoints, RLVR cut looped outputs from 126 to 29 pages (a 77 percent reduction), reduced outputs beyond the 9,000-token limit from 185 to 35, and raised the overall score from 66.24 to 71.38 (plus 5.18 on tables, plus 4.15 on charts). In a reference test on a synthetic dental form with an odontogram (256 held-out forms, 8 samples per page), pass@1 accuracy jumped from 0.00 percent to 95.85 percent after SFT and 96.58 percent after RLVR. These are dev-checkpoint results on synthetic forms of the same generator, not measurements on real-world noisy scans.


## DFlash2 Speculator Boosts Throughput 7.62x at Concurrency 1


The DFlash2 drafter is a separate 89.3-million-parameter model that proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, with about 14 accepted per verification step (approximately 15 tokens per step counting the target token). It includes a built-in MTP head with 1-token lookahead. In Nvidia's benchmark on one H200 in BF16 over 2,078 pages, DFlash2 delivered 7.62x speedup at concurrency 1 and 1.52x at concurrency 512, lifting throughput at 512 from 13.48 to 20.44 pages per second, compared to 2.98 for Parse 2.0. This translates to overall gains of 4.53x and 6.86x across the concurrency range.


Version 3.5 replaced the fixed 2048×1664 canvas with NaViT dynamic rectangular inputs, uses compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix, and employs GQA-8 (16 query, 8 key/value heads) for efficiency.


## Availability and Reproducible Recipe


The full recipe is open in the Nvidia NeMo GitHub repository (NVIDIA-NeMo/Nemotron), including paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, NeMo RL GRPO, vLLM candidate generation, and integration hooks for custom image-label pairs and verifiers. Teams can plug in their own domain data and train a specialized parser without starting from scratch.


The community has already adapted Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic, demonstrating the recipe's flexibility. Per the model card, ParseBench triple-pass scores 75.20 versus 75.10 for LightOnOCR-3-4B and 73.25 for Infinity-Parser2-Flash. Competitors are close on accuracy, but Nvidia's bet is speed: up to 20.44 pages per second on one H200, compared to 13.49 versus 2.76 for LightOnOCR.


## What This Means for RAG and Agent Teams


The release gives enterprise AI teams a commercial-grade, reproducible path to custom document parsing. With 18.88 million open training examples, a two-phase SFT-plus-RLVR pipeline, and a speculative-decoding drafter that hits 20.44 pages per second on a single H200, teams can now fine-tune Parse to their own forms, languages, and quality thresholds without negotiating per-model licenses or reverse-engineering proprietary training stacks. The benchmarks are synthetic, so accuracy on real-world noisy scans requires domain-specific validation, but the open recipe and commercial license remove the two biggest barriers to production deployment.
